title: Chart Spin — the same numbers, both ways
subtitle: One query, two opposite stories — plus four more ways a technically correct chart can lie: raw counts, rank charts, the wrong chart type, and axis order

source.publisher: Same DOHMH data as the Inspections tab — that is the point
source.note: One script, one run, one API call made both charts below. Nothing in the data was added, removed, or changed between them. Every difference is a display choice.

grain.row_is: one violation citation, rated per inspection
grain.note: The honest chart's window was fixed by the question before we looked at any data. The spun chart's window was hunted: we tried all 15 possible 12-month starts and kept the one that made Brooklyn's climb steepest. That choice leaves no trace in the picture. The last two charts push the lesson past framing into the chart itself — a raw count that ranks population, a rank chart that hides how big the gaps really are, and a map for a pattern with no geography.

charts.title: The honest render
charts.insight: Brooklyn is flat. Violations per inspection went 3.67 → 3.67 over the last twelve complete months. Its yearly drift (+0.19/yr) only ranks third, behind the Bronx (+0.32) and Manhattan (+0.23). All five boroughs sit inside one narrow band.
charts.form: Multi-line chart, zero baseline, one borough highlighted
charts.form_why: The claim was about change over time across boroughs, so time goes on x and every borough shares one y-scale. Highlighting Brooklyn and graying the rest is just emphasis. It points your eye without changing what any line shows.
charts.method: y-axis starts at zero so visible change equals real change. Window = last 12 complete calendar months, fixed by the question before we saw any data. No smoothing. Every line gets identical treatment. Partial current month excluded.
charts.caution: The real headline: the premise we were handed — 'Brooklyn is steadily rising while others stay flat' — turned out to be false. An honest chart can't make that claim, so this one doesn't.

charts.title: The spun render — same data, four levers moved
charts.insight: 'BROOKLYN VIOLATIONS SURGE 12 MONTHS RUNNING.' We built that headline from a 14% wobble in a dataset where the honest answer was +0.00. Nothing is made up. Every plotted value is real.
charts.form_why: Same chart, opposite conclusion — that's the whole point. Spin doesn't need a different chart type or a false number. It needs four choices that each sound defensible.
charts.method: 1) We cherry-picked the window: the max-slope option out of 15 candidates, starting at Brooklyn's trough. 2) We zoomed the y-axis to Brooklyn's own range, so a 14% change fills 100% of the panel — hiding behind the true rule that line charts don't have to start at zero. 3) We made the panel tall and narrow, which steepens any slope. Nobody audits aspect ratio. 4) We smoothed Brooklyn ONLY, with a three-month average (disclosed at 5.5pt), so its clean line reads as signal while the raw grays read as noise.
charts.caution: Every one of these choices has a legitimate use, and each could be defended in a meeting by quoting a real principle. That's how charts lie in real life — far more common than fake data, and much harder to catch.

charts.title: Watch it happen — the honest chart becomes the spun one, one lever at a time
charts.insight: Six display decisions separate the two charts above. Nothing else. This piece pins one chart to your screen and fires the levers one by one as you scroll — baseline, window, aspect, smoothing, color, title. Brooklyn stays 3.67 → 3.67 the whole time. The last step undoes everything at once to prove it.
charts.form: Scrollytelling — a pinned chart you transform by scrolling
charts.form_why: A gallery can only tell you the honest and spun charts share the same data. A scroll piece shows you: you watch the change happen, and you can scroll back to any point. The pattern and the trigger library (scrollama.js, MIT) come from The Pudding, who open-source the machinery behind their visual essays.
charts.method: The chart renders in your browser from borough-series.json — the same numbers the PNGs were drawn from, exported by the same guarded pull under the same watermark. Six of this tab's seven levers fire, one per step. The seventh — how the data gets drawn — is covered by the map and bump chart below. JavaScript off? You get the static side-by-side instead.
charts.caution: The order of the steps is itself a display choice. Firing the levers one at a time suggests they work alone. In a real spun chart they arrive together and reinforce each other — and the piece says so right on the page instead of leaving it unsaid.

charts.title: Side by side — every axis labeled, and the right panel still lies
charts.insight: Labels don't save you. Both panels carry full axis labels and their own disclosure line, and the deception survives anyway. It lives in the frame, not in anything a label can name.
charts.form_why: Equal panels keep the comparison about the levers and nothing else. An earlier version drew the spun panel narrower — keeping its aspect trick — so you couldn't tell 'the y-axis is zoomed' apart from 'the panel is squished'. The comparison was guilty of the very thing it teaches.
charts.method: Left and right render from the same array of numbers in the same script run. Only three things differ: y-range, window, and which line got smoothed.
charts.caution: 'The axes are labeled, just read them' is the standard defense of a spun chart. This image breaks it. Window, y-range, aspect ratio, and one-sided smoothing have no axis labels — so a reader who checks only the labels has checked nothing.

charts.title: Raw counts rank by size — and rank charts hide how small the gap is
charts.insight: The claim wasn't even right on its own terms. A founder said Queens had the worst inspection problem 'because it recorded the most critical violations.' Manhattan actually has the most (18,487 vs 13,253). Queens does lead both fair metrics — but the other four boroughs sit within 3% of each other, and Queens is only 9% above that cluster.
charts.form: Bump chart across three ways of counting
charts.form_why: On the findings tab this chart answers whether the claim survives. Here it shows two display traps at once. First, the founder's own chart — a bar of raw counts — was a population census dressed up as a problem: count raw totals across groups of different sizes and you rank the sizes. Second, and more uncomfortable: THIS chart has its own trap. Bump charts show rank, and rank makes a hairline gap look like a landslide. A 2% difference and a 40% difference draw the exact same line crossing.
charts.method: We print the value at every node to defuse the rank illusion. We build the caption from the cluster shape, not from the single biggest gap, so 'Queens is rank 1' and 'the lead is modest' can't contradict each other on the same image. An earlier draft used a global spread stat and hit exactly that contradiction.
charts.caution: Fixing one distortion can create the opposite one. The founder's raw count oversold Queens's problem; a rank-only chart would have oversold the correction. And neither way of dividing is automatically fairer — per-inspection reflects enforcement policy, per-restaurant mixes in how long each place has been around to be inspected. What you divide by has to follow the decision you're making.

charts.title: The wrong form: a map for a pattern that isn't spatial
charts.insight: This pattern has no 'where.' A stakeholder asked for a map titled 'Where frequent inspections cause worse outcomes.' But the link is 98% non-geographic — pooled slope +5.75, zip-demeaned slope +5.64 — so neighborhoods explain about 2% of it. The map they asked for would have put a 'where' on something that has no where.
charts.form: Residual scatter map — a map demoted on purpose
charts.form_why: Maps persuade because every dot is real — and that's exactly the risk. A map can show WHERE things line up, never WHY, and this claim was pure why. So instead of refusing the map, we demoted it to the one job it can honestly do here: show what geography still explains after cuisine and neighborhood averages are removed. It comes out salt-and-pepper, no clusters. That emptiness is the answer.
charts.method: Severity minus the cuisine average minus the neighborhood average, one dot per restaurant. 20,092 restaurants; 313 excluded for missing or (0,0) coordinates — counted, not silently dropped. Aspect ratio set to roughly cos(latitude) so New York isn't stretched. An ignored aspect ratio is its own distortion.
charts.caution: The requested title said 'cause' before any analysis had earned it. Worse, the arrow runs backward here: risk-based enforcement sends more inspections to worse restaurants. A title that names its conclusion in advance turns the chart into an illustration of a decision already made.

charts.title: Axis order is a causal claim — even when the title says otherwise
charts.insight: Scoring worse gets you inspected more. Restaurants in the A range (0–13) average 1.04 inspections; those scoring 41+ average 2.18. The jump starts right at 14 — exactly where DOHMH's re-inspection rule kicks in.
charts.form: Bucketed line, cause on x and effect on y
charts.form_why: You read x → y as cause → effect in the first two seconds, before any title. The Inspections tab's facet chart puts inspections on x and score on y, so its LAYOUT argues 'inspections make restaurants worse' — backwards from what actually drives it. Rewriting that chart's title fixed the words. This chart fixes the grammar. Same data, same window, same grain: only the axes swapped.
charts.method: One point per restaurant — its worst score and its inspection count — bucketed into DOHMH's own grading bands, not cut points we invented. n printed at every point. Zero baseline, on purpose: an earlier render started the y-axis at 1.0 and let the 1.04→2.18 climb fill the whole panel. That's the y-zoom lever from two charts above this one.
charts.caution: Swapping the axes does NOT prove cause. It just lines the chart's grammar up with a mechanism we already know from the written enforcement rule. Without that rule, this chart would imply the reverse just as easily. The honesty comes from the documented policy, not the axis order.

cannot_answer: Whether any particular published chart was spun on purpose. These four levers are also the everyday choices of honest charting. Intent doesn't show up in the output — which is exactly why disclosure matters more than motive.
Whether a chart is trustworthy from the chart alone. Two of these levers — the window hunt and the one-sided smoothing — leave no visible trace at all. You need the method, not just the image.

How to make a truly neutral chart. There isn't one. Every chart picks a window, a baseline, an aspect ratio, a smoothing policy, colors, and a caption. Honest charts disclose those choices — they don't avoid making them.
Whether these five are all the ways a chart can mislead. They aren't. They're the ones we hit while building this site — including two we introduced ourselves and had to fix.
